surfaces.part: top compartment (empty light back panel with a few books at right)
book rows with spines facing the viewer

answer.evidence: The whole 32px-wide body is a flat face-on elevation. Row 1 is the dark outline. Row 2 is a 1-row light rim. Rows 3-7 are a light back panel of the top compartment, with book spines standing upright in front of it at the right. That makes it a vertical open compartment, not a top surface. Row 8 is a grey line and row 9 is dark, which is the underside edge of the top board and the shadow over the first book row. The rest is stacked book rows at rows 10-13, 17-20 and 24-28. Each is separated by a 1-2 row light shelf edge (rows 14-15, 21-23) and a dark shadow. These shelf boards are thin face-on strips, not foreshortened horizontal planes. There is no ellipse, roof or visible contents seen from above, and no receding side face. So there is a front face of about 30 rows but no real top, as in the red 'bookshelf' reference.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a standing furniture piece, so it matches the reference kind. Measured facts support it: 20 visible tones per 16x16 tile, level with prop-well-roofed (20) and above prop-stall-cheese (17) and prop-hedge (9). Near-flat coverage is 0%, and 0% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is tinted rather than a black sticker line. By eye, the cabinet frame steps through about 5 lightness levels, from a pale highlight through grey-blue mids to a dark blue-grey edge. The interior rows are broken up by many small, varied book spines, which gives dense texture and avoids large flat areas. The panel surfaces are somewhat smoother than the references' grain and tile scallops, so texture is rated 'some' rather than 'rich'. A careful artist would still accept it next to the references without it looking thinner or flatter.
